items.title: AI Journey: The Path to Safe and Productive AI Use
items.summary:
Artificial intelligence is transforming work practices, processes, and business models faster than any other technology in recent decades. The question is no longer whether AI will be used, but how consciously we manage its use: Which use cases create measurable added value? What data should be fed into AI systems? And who is responsible for the results, risks, and decisions?

  • Those who wait too long will lose practical experience, valuable know-how, and possibly competitive advantages.

  • Those who implement AI without clear rules simultaneously open up new vulnerabilities: Confidential information can leak unchecked into external services, flawed results can influence decisions, and regulatory requirements can fall by the wayside.

A structured AI journey bridges these two perspectives. It outlines the step-by-step path to productive, secure, and transparent AI usage.
Good AI governance supports innovation. It clarifies responsibilities, protects sensitive data, and creates the framework within which teams can safely develop, test, and deploy AI applications.

items.title: [Alert] PHP2Shell: Critical PHP RCEs – Patch Now and Check for Signs of an Attack
Trusted. Deceived. Compromised. How Security Awareness Protects Against Phishing
items.summary: Social engineering works because attackers deliberately exploit human routines, trust, and time pressure. A sender address that appears familiar, a familiar writing style, or a plausibly placed link can quickly make a message seem legitimate. If the deception succeeds, it can lead to a chain of attacks: Attackers first compromise an account or environment and then use existing business relationships to launch further phishing attacks.

items.title: Claude is new to the team – and hasn't been given any onboarding.
items.summary:
Many companies in the DACH region have recently welcomed a new team member. This person is exceptionally energetic, works across multiple teams and departments at the same time—and depending on which floor you’re on, goes by a different name. Most of the time, it’s Claude. Sometimes Codex. In one team we recently worked with, the newcomer was named Hermes.

You run into them in the hallway, at stand-ups, in the break room:

“I worked with Claude to customize my Excel spreadsheet.”
“Codex built me a new interface for my Access database.”
“Hermes now automatically organizes all my calendar entries.”

These aren’t quotes from a study. These are statements we’ve been hearing for weeks in our projects and long-term engagements, from people who don’t work in IT, but in financial control, sales, and customer service.

Claude is just one example. The AI model Claude, developed by Anthropic, is based on a Large Language Model (LLM) and has long been capable of more than just generating text: It develops applications, automates processes, and can collaborate with other tools. This makes it increasingly possible for people who have never developed software or automated processes themselves to create their own applications.

As a result, AI assistants are changing the way we work. What used to require a development assignment, a budget, or months of project time can now be accomplished in just a few hours using AI coding tools and Vibe Coding.

items.title: MDR and AI: Why Expertise and Data Sovereignty are Crucial
items.summary: The current cybersecurity landscape is making it increasingly difficult for security professionals to detect attacks early and classify them correctly. AI-powered reconnaissance, exploit generation, and lateral movement within compromised environments are now part of the operational reality. At the same time, “Living-off-the-Land (LOTL)” techniques—which involve the misuse of legitimate system tools—along with cloud-based infrastructures and automated attack chains, make detection more difficult.

items.title: OT Asset Discovery: Best Practices for Secure OT Inventory Management
items.summary: In industrial environments, there is often no complete overview of the OT systems in use. Older or undocumented components, network structures that have evolved over the years, connections between IT and OT, and external access points can result in parts of the OT infrastructure not being included in the current asset inventory. As a result, potential attack vectors and dependencies may remain undetected under certain circumstances.

items.summary: Compared to the report on the second quarter of 2026, the geopolitical cyber landscape has become significantly clearer in the third quarter. What was still described in Q2/26 as a risk of escalation and geographic expansion is now evident in confirmed incidents with physical consequences and official attributions.

items.title: Cybersecurity Put to the Test: How Compliant Is Your Company, Really?
items.summary: Safety measures may be in place, processes may be defined, and regulatory requirements may be known. What matters is whether they actually achieve the desired state of safety in practice. The gap between assumptions and the verifiable actual state becomes particularly relevant when new requirements, technical changes, or business decisions call for a robust assessment of the current situation.

items.title: AI Analyses in the SOC: How Random Samples Enable Targeted Monitoring
items.summary: AI now writes safety analyses. In the SOC, language models generate the initial draft. They summarize security data, identify patterns, and propose an initial assessment in seconds—tasks that would take experts significantly longer to complete. This shifts the focus. Today, the key question is how to reliably verify whether the AI analysis is correct.

items.title: Certificate Revocation: When 24 Hours Affect Availability
items.summary:
Digital certificates are a key foundation for secure digital communication. They enable websites, applications, devices, and services to verify identities and establish encrypted connections. As long as a certificate is valid and trustworthy, this process usually runs invisibly in the background.

But trust can change. If, for example, a private key is compromised or a certificate is issued incorrectly or without authorization, it must be revoked. And in that case, the regular expiration date no longer matters: depending on the cause, the deadline for revocation may be as short as 24 hours.

For companies, this means that, in addition to ever-shorter certificate validity periods, a second factor is becoming increasingly relevant: the ability to replace certificates very quickly and in a controlled manner in the event of an emergency. Without transparency and automated processes, a certificate issue can quickly turn into an availability and business risk.

This article explains the current requirements for certificate revocation, when the 24-hour deadline applies, and why automated certificate lifecycle management plays a crucial role in this process.
